summary: Right footprint and recognisable hex-net goal, but clean CG: the net is drum-tight, the rear frame is a different, unpainted-looking material, and nothing at the ground joins.
critique: The 7.32 x 2.44 m mouth and the posts (roughly 100-120 mm) read as the right scale. The angled side stanchions and low rear ground bar give the classic shape. Problems: (1) The net is stretched flat on every plane like a fence, with no sag in the roof, no billow at the back and no slack lying on the ground at the bottom bar. A real net hangs 100-300 mm low between supports and bunches at the base. (2) The front posts and crossbar are bright matte white, but the stanchions and rear bar are thin, mid-grey, slightly metallic tubes. They look like a different product bolted on. Real goals either paint the stanchions white or use dull galvanised steel, and the tube is 40-50 mm, not wire-thin. (3) Nothing joins: no net hooks or clips on the posts or bar (goal.box has them), no corner brackets or welded elbows where the stanchions meet the crossbar, and no ground sockets or collars where the posts enter the turf. (4) Materials are uniform, with no grime band at the foot of the posts, no scuffs, and no specular variation on the white paint.
suggestions: Add net sag. Lower the roof-net vertices with a catenary of 150-250 mm between supports. Push the back panel out 100-200 mm at mid-height. Let the bottom 300 mm of the back panel lie flat on the ground behind the rear bar. This is vertex displacement only, at zero extra triangles.

Unify the frame. Give the stanchions and rear bar a 45-50 mm diameter and the same white paint (albedo ~0.80, roughness 0.45) as the posts, or a deliberate dull galvanised finish (albedo 0.55, metallic 1, roughness 0.6) across the whole rear frame.

Add hardware: net hooks every ~250 mm along the posts and crossbar (instanced 8-tri hook, ~60 instances), a cast corner bracket at each stanchion/crossbar junction (~100 tris each), and a 120 mm ground collar at each post foot.
Add wear in a small 256 px mask: a 50-80 mm green/brown grass stain band at the post bases, and faint scuffs at ball height on the inner post faces.
Give the net cord a slight off-white albedo (~0.70) and more thickness variation, so it doesn't read as a CG wireframe at distance.
renderer_notes: The net casts almost no shadow while the frame casts a hard one. That is alpha-tested shadow casting, not the asset.

summary: A readable, playful survey stake with a nice paint-drip detail, but oversized, too clean-cut and sitting on an odd soil mound.
critique: The orange-dipped top with drips, the nail in the top and the pink flagging tape are the right ingredients. Problems: (1) Scale and section. It reads as a 75-100 mm square post, probably 0.6-0.8 m tall. A typical UK survey peg is a 50 x 50 mm (or 25 x 50 mm) sawn softwood stake, 300-600 mm long, with only 150-300 mm left above ground. (2) The timber is perfectly square with a vertical stripe texture. There are no sawn-face fibres, no arris damage, no hammer-flattened, split or mushroomed top, and no darker damp or soil staining at the base. (3) The flagging tape is a flat rigid band, perfectly horizontal, with a single stiff tail that looks like a plastic sheet. Real tape is knotted, twisted, and has two thin streamers that curl and hang irregularly. Its saturated hot pink is also brighter than real fluorescent pink in daylight. (4) The heaped soil mound is about 3-4x the peg footprint and looks like a molehill. A driven peg leaves at most a small scuffed ring. The mound also has a hard, flat-coloured outline against the grass.
suggestions: Rescale to 50 x 50 mm section and ~450 mm overall, with ~250 mm exposed. Add a 30-40 mm pointed tip below ground (hidden, for LOD) and slightly bevel or chip the arrises (+~40 tris).
Deform the top: flatten or mushroom it 2-3 mm, and add a hairline split down one face from the nail. Darken the bottom 60 mm (wet soil stain, albedo x0.6).

Remodel the tape. Make a 25 mm wide twisted loop with a knot bump, and two 150-250 mm streamers as thin bent ribbons with 4-6 segments each and a little twist (~60 tris). Use fluorescent pink albedo ~(0.95,0.35,0.6) with roughness 0.5, so it doesn't look like glowing plastic.
Replace the mound with a 150-200 mm scuffed soil ring that blends into the grass via a vertex-alpha or decal falloff, or drop it entirely and let the ground system handle it.
Add sawn-timber grain and pencil or marker writing (chainage or level, e.g. 'CH 120 / +0.35') as a tiny decal on one face. It sells authenticity for almost no cost.

summary: Convincing Heras-type panel with correct round-top frame, couplers and rubber feet; mesh and frame are a little too clean and the feet are simplified.
critique: The proportions match the reference (~3.5 x 2.0 m), with rounded top corners, a centre vertical stay, coupler lugs on the uprights, two recycled-rubber feet and a mottled galvanised frame. This is close to a realistic model. Shortfalls: (1) The mesh looks like a flat grid of lines with no wire thickness or weld nodes, and it is perfectly regular and planar. Real panels have visible welded wire with slight waviness, and the mesh is welded to the inside face of the frame. (2) The frame tube looks right but the bottom rail seems to sit on top of the feet. In reality the panel uprights drop into the cast holes in the foot, with ~50-100 mm of upright below the bottom rail. (3) The feet are featureless boxes with soft bevels. Real feet have two leg holes, moulded ribs, a hand-hold slot and a recycled-rubber speckle. (4) The coupler lugs are only on one side. The paired clamp (two half-shells and a bolt) between adjacent panels is missing, and there is no anti-lift or stabiliser stay option. (5) There is no wear: no white zinc oxide, rust at the welds, mud on the feet, or cable-tied banner remnants.
suggestions: Make the mesh an alpha-tested card with a normal map that shows 4 mm wire and weld nodes at about 75 x 250 mm aperture (or the anti-climb 50 x 50). Offset it 15 mm inside the frame and add slight per-panel bow. Cost: 1 quad and a 512 px tileable.

Extend the uprights 80 mm below the bottom rail into the feet. Model the feet with two leg-hole recesses, 3 ribs per side and a chamfered top (~150 tris each). Use albedo 0.06-0.08 with grey speckle, roughness 0.85, and mud on the lower third.
Add an optional instanced coupler-clamp prop (two shells, bolt; ~120 tris) at the top and bottom of the shared upright, and a diagonal stabiliser stay variant.
Add wear: white-rust blooms and orange rust at the weld points (mask-driven), and a few torn zip ties on the top rail as random instances.
Allow a slight random lean (0.5-1.5 deg) and a small height offset per instance, so long runs don't look CAD-perfect.

summary: Recognisable mid-size SUV with nice wheels, roof rails and plate, but the front end is malformed and the body surfacing is flat and lumpy.
critique: Scale and overall stance are plausible for a Qashqai/Evoque-class car (~4.4 x 1.8 x 1.6 m), and the wheels, roof rails, UK plates, light signatures and mirrors are all there. Problems: (1) The front end is broken. The bonnet's leading corners crumple into pinched 'ears' above the headlamps (clearly visible in the 3/4 view). The bonnet front edge pokes forward into a beak in the side view, overhanging the bumper. The bonnet also dips sharply toward the nose, so the car looks melted. (2) The body sides are a single flat slab with no shoulder line, no wheel-arch flares or cladding, and no tumblehome. The glasshouse sits on the body with no taper. A modern SUV has a strong shoulder crease, ~100-150 mm of tumblehome and black plastic arch mouldings. (3) The windscreen meets the bonnet at a dark flat cowl that is too wide and too flat, and the A-pillar is too upright relative to the bonnet line. (4) The windows are uniformly dark with almost no reflection. There are no visible door handles, and the door shut lines are faint. (5) The paint has no clearcoat response. The navy reads as plastic, with no orange-peel or roughness variation and no dirt on the sills or arches. (6) The grille is a large flat mesh rectangle with an invented badge. That's fine, but it sits flush with no depth.
suggestions: Fix the bonnet first. Clamp the bonnet front corners to the headlamp top surface (no vertices above or ahead of the bumper skin). Keep the bonnet leading edge 20-40 mm behind the bumper face and make the bonnet surface rise monotonically from nose to cowl, about 0.85 m at the nose to 1.0 m at the cowl.

Add a shoulder: a 10-15 mm crease line running from the headlamp to the tail-lamp at belt-line height minus ~80 mm. Inset the side glass and pillars by 80-120 mm at the roof (tumblehome). That is about +400 tris in the body loop.
Add black textured arch cladding and sill mouldings (albedo 0.04, roughness 0.8), with arches flared 20-30 mm beyond the door skin. This breaks up the flat lower sides cheaply.

Paint: a clearcoat-like setup (base roughness 0.35, metallic 0.5 flake approximation, or a second specular lobe if the shader supports it). Add a tiling road-grime mask on the lower 250 mm, plus a dirtier rear hatch.

Recess the grille 20-30 mm behind the bumper skin and add door handles (6 instanced ~40-tri parts). Darken the shut lines in a 512 px trim normal. Give the glass a cheap fresnel env tint so it isn't black.
renderer_notes: Without screen-space reflections or an environment probe, glass and paint look flatter than they would with reflections. Some of the dull paint is the renderer, but the geometry faults are the asset.

summary: Strong silver-birch character with pendulous foliage and white bark, but the crown is lopsided and sparse, the bark lacks markings, and the branches are straight cylinders.
critique: The weeping-birch read is good: a white trunk with a dark base, upswept limbs, and hanging strands of small diamond-shaped leaves. The dappled shadow is convincing. Shortfalls: (1) The crown is split into two or three detached clumps with a bare gap. From the side it is one-sided and almost flat-topped. A mature Betula pendula (15-25 m, spread 6-8 m) has an ovoid crown with a leading central stem to the top. This one looks closer to 10-12 m tall, with a narrow trunk that is about right. (2) The bark is uniform white from base to crown. A birch has black diamond-shaped lenticel bands and horizontal striping, and the lower 1-2 m is rough, fissured and dark grey-black, not a neat black collar. (3) In the close-up the branches are straight, smooth, bright-white cylinders with abrupt joins and no taper. Birch twigs are dark red-brown to purplish and very fine, and only the larger limbs are white. (4) The leaf cards are visible as separate strands with too-even spacing, and the leaves are a single bright green with no translucency variation or yellowing.
suggestions: Regrow the crown with a central leader to ~90% of the height and branch whorls around 360 deg. Constrain the crown envelope to an ovoid of ~6-7 m spread so there are no gaps wider than ~1 m. Keep 8-15 primary limbs and droop the outer twigs.

Bark: a 1024 x 2048 trunk texture with horizontal lenticel dashes and black diamond scars at branch scars, blending to fissured near-black bark (albedo ~0.08) over the bottom 1.5 m with a noisy, not banded, transition.

Taper the branches (radius x0.6 per generation), bend each segment 5-15 deg, and add a branch collar where it meets the parent. Shift twig albedo from white to red-brown (0.25,0.15,0.12) beyond generation 2.

Leaf cards: vary hue (+/-8%) and value per card, add 5-10% yellowing, and enable back-face translucency or a wrap-diffuse term. Randomise strand length (0.3-1.2 m) and twist so curtains don't read as evenly spaced.
Budget: keep ~3-5k tris for LOD0 with ~150-250 strand cards. LOD1 can be 40 crossed cards, and LOD2 an impostor billboard.

summary: Convincing compact tandem roller with good parts inventory (ROPS, beacon, seat, wheel, drums, scrapers, decals); proportions and detailing are a bit simple and clean.
critique: This reads clearly as a 1.2 m twin-drum roller in the Bomag BW 120 class. It has a fold-style ROPS hoop with work lights and an amber beacon, a suspension seat, a steering wheel, drum scrapers, hazard chevrons, a fictional brand 'VIBROMAC TR120 AD' decal and a light grime pass. That is a realistic-model score. Shortfalls: (1) The drums look a bit small and have prominent wheel-like hub faces. A BW 120 drum is ~570 mm diameter and 1200 mm wide, and its face is mostly hidden by the rubber-mounted drum yoke frame, with the vibration motor bulge on one side. (2) The articulation joint between the front and rear frames is not visible. The centre platform looks like a flat plate floating between the two bonnets. (3) The bonnets are clean rounded boxes with no louvres. They need the engine-air grille, tank caps and lifting eyes, and a proper water tank on the front frame with spray bars over each drum. (4) The ROPS is plain square tube with no hinge plates for the fold, and the seat sits without a visible console. (5) Wear is light. Rollers are caked in tack coat and bitumen spatter around the drums, scrapers and lower body, and the drums themselves are polished bright where they contact the ground.
suggestions: Add a visible articulation joint: a ~200 mm hinge block with two vertical pins and a steering ram (~250 tris). Push the operator platform into the rear frame so it isn't floating.

Drums: 570 mm diameter, 1200 mm width. Cover the outer face with a yoke plate and rubber buffer blocks (4 per side, instanced), and add a hydraulic motor housing on one side. Make the rolling surface polished steel (metallic 1, roughness 0.25) with dark bitumen streaks at the edges.
Add spray bars (a thin tube with nozzles across each drum, ~80 tris each), water tank fill caps, engine grille louvres as a normal-map trim on the rear bonnet side, and two lifting eyes on top.
Add ROPS fold hinges at mid-height (two plate pairs and pins) and a bracket console under the seat.
Wear: a mask-driven black bitumen spatter on the lower 400 mm of the body and the scrapers, and faded, chipped yellow (albedo 0.62,0.50,0.05) on the edges and step plates. Use a 1k shared trim atlas.

summary: Clean, correctly sized box goal with full white frame and net clips; let down by a perfectly taut cage-like net and no wear or ground interface.
critique: The frame is consistent white tube with a rear top bar and rear verticals. The 7.32 x 2.44 m mouth and ~2 m depth look right, and the net clips along the crossbar are a good detail. The hex net reads well up close. Problems: (1) The net is stretched planar on all five faces, like a cage. Real box-goal nets still sag between the rear frame members, bunch at the rear corners and lie on the ground at the back, and the roof net dips noticeably. (2) The net cord is very thin and uniform pure white. At mid-distance it reads as a shaded wireframe, not a nylon cord with thickness and slight fuzz. (3) There is no ground interface: no sockets or collars at the posts, no ground anchors or pegs on the rear bottom bar, no net weights. (4) The surfaces are pristine, with no grass stain at the bases, no scuffs, and no welds or end caps at the corners. The corner joints are simple mitred tubes with no corner castings.
suggestions: Displace the net vertices so the roof sags 150-200 mm at its centre, the back panel bows out 100 mm, and the bottom 200-300 mm of the back and sides drapes on the turf. This is vertex-only.

Use a slightly thicker cord with off-white albedo ~0.72, roughness 0.8, and cord-radius variation in the alpha texture so it holds up at 20-40 m without shimmering. Generate mips with coverage preservation.
Add a corner casting at each crossbar/upright and rear junction (~80 tris each) and ground collars at the post feet. Add 4 instanced ground pegs or anchor plates on the rear bar.
Add a small wear mask: a grass-stain band at the post bases and faint ball scuffs on the crossbar underside.
renderer_notes: The net's shadow is mostly missing (only the frame shadows), which is alpha-shadow handling in the viewer.

summary: Good stand layout vocabulary (seat lettering, vomitories, aisles, handrails, terrace with crush barriers) but seats and concrete are blocky and uniform.
critique: There is strong content for a classic UK ground: two-tier main stand with 'THE BLUES' seat lettering, a vomitory recess, aisle stairs with handrails, and a standing/safe-standing terrace with crush barriers at one end. Shortfalls: (1) The seats read as small tinted blocks with no visible tip-up pan/back form or shadow under the pan. At normal viewing distances they are noisy blue speckle rather than rows. (2) All concrete (risers, treads, stair flights, vomitory walls) is one flat beige-grey value, with no staining, drainage streaks, painted step nosings (yellow or white edges are standard in UK grounds) or gum or wear. (3) The terrace barriers are thin, uniform and not quite consistent in height. There are no barrier stanchion feet, and the steps look the same height as seated risers. (4) The fascia between tiers is a plain dark-blue band with no signage, a TV gantry or a front balustrade glass/steel detail. (5) The end-stand seating meets the corner with a hard diagonal cut and no corner infill or exit stair.
suggestions: Use a 2-LOD seat: ~60-tri tip-up (pan, back, two brackets) within 40 m, and a normal-mapped seat-row strip card beyond. That gives the seat the dark gap under the pan that sells rows at distance.
Paint step nosings: a 50 mm yellow or white stripe on every aisle step and the tread edge in a shared 256 px trim. Add vertical rain-streak and dirt decals on risers below the barrier rails.
Crush barriers: 1.1 m high, 48 mm top rail on 60 mm stanchions with base plates every 2-3 m, staggered between rows, and galvanised material with rust spots.
Add tier-front detail: a 1.1 m front wall with a steel handrail, sponsor lettering on the fascia, and a small TV/press gantry slung under the upper tier.
Vary the seat albedo slightly per seat (+/-5%) and sprinkle 1-2% faded or broken seats, so blocks don't read as a uniform tint.

summary: Correct roof types (cantilevered truss stands, column-supported main stand) with decent underside trusses, but the top surfaces are flat slabs with no sheeting profile or edge detail.
critique: The underside framing on the side stands, with lattice rafters, purlins and posts, is convincing from pitch level, and the main stand's front-column roof is period-appropriate. Problems: (1) From above, every roof is a plain light-grey slab with two lighter stripes. There is no trapezoidal profiled sheeting, no rooflight strip pattern, no ridge capping, no gutters or downpipes, and no weathering such as streaks below fixings or moss at the low edge. (2) The black fascia on the corner stand is a thick flat beam with no flashing or gutter profile, and it cuts across the corner at an odd angle. (3) The main-stand front columns are very large white cylinders, about 600 mm or more, with no base plates, cross-bracing or connection to the roof beam. Classic UK column stands use smaller I-section or tube columns with knee braces. (4) The rooftop boxes (plant or vents) are plain cubes.
suggestions: Apply a tiling normal and roughness map of 32/1000 trapezoidal sheeting (crest pitch 333 mm) to the top surfaces. Add rooflight strips of translucent sheeting every ~3-4 bays. This is texture only.

Add a gutter box section (300 x 200 mm) along the rear and front edges, with downpipes every 10-15 m on the facade. Add a rain-streak and grime gradient decal running from the ridge to the front edge.
Shrink the main-stand columns to 250-350 mm, or use an I-section. Add a base plate, a capital or knee brace to the roof beam, and white paint with rust bleed at the bolts.
Replace plain rooftop cubes with louvred plant housings (normal-map trim) and add a walkway with edge-protection rails on the larger roofs.

summary: Brick facade gives a UK-ground flavour, but the main stand rear is a monolithic 5-6 storey grid of identical windows that reads as an office or mill block, and the plaza is empty.
critique: Problems: (1) Scale and massing. The main stand rear is as tall as the roof ridge, with five or six identical storeys of punched windows, which looks like a warehouse or hotel. Classic UK main stands (Leitch-style) have a brick rear that is roughly 2-3 storeys of offices or lounges, with the roof and seating rake visible above or behind, plus gables, a central entrance or club crest, and pediments. (2) The windows repeat identically with no sills, lintels, frames or reveals, and there is no variation in glazing or blinds. (3) The brick is a flat red-brown with almost no mortar read at distance, and no plinth course, string courses, stone dressings or weathering. (4) The corner where the facade meets the end stand is a blank brick triangular wedge. (5) The turnstile blocks are tiny boxes spaced along the base, with no 'TURNSTILES' signage, gates, ticket office or club shop frontage. (6) The concourse and plaza is one flat grey slab with scattered trees, with no paving pattern, kerbs, bollards, crowd barriers or lighting columns.
suggestions: Cut the facade to 2-3 storeys (~9-12 m). Show the rear of the seating rake or a clad rear wall above it, and add a central feature bay with a gable or parapet, club crest and name lettering.
Window module: add a 100 mm stone or concrete sill and lintel, a 60 mm frame, 100 mm reveal depth (in a normal map or a small inset), and per-window glazing tint or blind variation from an atlas.
Brick: a 1024 px tiling brick with mortar normal, a blue-engineering-brick plinth course of 600 mm, a stone string course per floor, and soot or rain streak decals below the sills.
Turnstile banks: 6-8 grouped doors with red/blue painted steel shutters, a 'TURNSTILES 1-8' sign, an overhang canopy and queue barriers. Add a glazed club shop or ticket office frontage at one end.
Concourse: a paving tile texture with a kerb edge, bollards, lighting columns and a few waste bins (all instanced kit props).

summary: Classic corner lattice pylons with tilted lamp heads read very well as a traditional UK ground; head and base detail are simplified.
critique: This is a good choice of typology: four tall tapering lattice towers with angled rectangular heads holding a grid of lamps, at about the right height for a lower-league ground (30-40 m). The lattice reads well against the sky. Shortfalls: (1) The lamp head is a flat panel of identical small squares, with no individual lamp housings with visors, no walkway or platform with handrails behind the head, and no ladder. (2) The lattice members are uniform thickness, and the tower base has no concrete plinth, holding-down bolts, cable access door or perimeter fencing. (3) The towers are a uniform pale grey with no galvanised mottling, rust or bird guano. (4) The lamp face shows no emissive or glass differentiation, so at night it would have no believable lamp lenses.
suggestions: Build the head as 4-6 rows of instanced lamp housings (a rectangular box with a hood visor, ~40 tris each, 24-48 per head) on a frame, with a 0.8 m service walkway, handrail and access ladder up the tower face (instanced rungs).
Use heavier corner legs (2x the bracing tube diameter) and add a 1.5 m concrete plinth with base plates and bolt heads, a cable entry box and a small fence.
Use a galvanised material (metallic 1, roughness 0.55, albedo 0.6) with a low-frequency zinc mottle and orange rust at the joints, via a cheap world-space noise mask.
Give each lamp housing a glass face with fresnel and an emissive channel, so the same mesh works lit at night.

summary: Good pitch read with mowing pattern, crisp markings and believable goalmouth/centre wear; the checkerboard is too regular and the goal nets are taut.
critique: Markings are crisp and to scale. Worn sandy goalmouth, centre-circle and linesman-channel patches are a strong, believable detail, and the goals are correctly sized with hex nets. Shortfalls: (1) The mowing pattern is a perfect, equal-contrast checkerboard. Real stadium pitches use stripes or a subtle checker, with contrast that changes with view direction (the lean of the grass), and here it looks like a tiled texture. (2) The line paint has no breakup or slight width wobble and no paint on blades. At pitch level it reads as decal-perfect. (3) The wear patches are blurry blobs, with no divots, sand top-dressing grain or scuffed transition. (4) The goal nets are drum-tight (see goal.box), and there is no net-support stanchion or back ground anchors. (5) The pitch apron between the touchline and the boards is the same grass, with no artificial-turf strip or drainage channel, which is normal in UK stadia.
suggestions: Drive the mowing contrast by view angle (sheen ∝ dot(view, stripe direction)), at ±6-10% value, so stripes flip light or dark as the camera turns. This is a shader-only change.
Add line breakup with a 512 px noise mask on line alpha (±5% width, small gaps) and slight green bleed. Feather the edge over ~10 mm.
Give the wear patches a sand/soil albedo with a grain texture, scattered divot decals and a noisy edge transition, and concentrate them in the 6-yard box and the linesman's run.
Add a 2-3 m artificial-turf or tarmac apron strip and a slot drain behind the touchline. This is cheap and reads as 'stadium'.

summary: Correctly placed dugouts flanking a tunnel mouth, but both are blocky boxes with flat colours and no glazing, technical area or tunnel detail.
critique: Layout is right: two dugouts either side of a central tunnel on the halfway line, with blue seats inside and the technical area markings on the grass. Problems: (1) The dugouts are open-fronted rectangular boxes with thick red side walls, a flat teal slab roof and no transparent side panels. Typical UK stadium dugouts are polycarbonate or perspex shells, curved or angled, or brick bases with clear perspex sides and roof so spectators can see through. (2) There is no trim, no bench backing, no kit bags or water bottles, and no club crest or sponsor on the dugout. (3) The tunnel is a grey box with a double door and a pink header slab. It needs a retractable/telescopic tunnel or at least a walled tunnel mouth with steps down, padding, handrails, the 'home/away' signage and an overhead canopy. (4) The teal box beside the left dugout (fourth-official board or a cool box?) is an untextured cube. (5) Every surface is a flat colour with no edge bevels or wear.
suggestions: Rebuild the dugouts as a 6-8 m shell: a steel frame (50 mm tubes) with curved or angled transparent polycarbonate roof and side panels (alpha 0.25, roughness 0.1, slight tint), on a 300 mm brick or concrete plinth. Keep 2 rows of padded club seats inside (instanced). Around 1-1.5k tris each.

Tunnel: a telescopic concourse tunnel (ribbed fabric or perspex segments, ~3 m wide, extending 4-6 m onto the apron) in club colour, or a stepped walled mouth with padded blue walls, handrails and a crest on the header.
Add a fourth-official desk with a monitor and a substitution board prop, technical-area cones, and water crates and kit bags as instanced dressing.
Bevel all box edges by 10-20 mm and add a 512 px painted-steel/brick wear set (scuffs at the base, rain streaks).

summary: Well-designed fictional sponsor boards and a convincing scoreboard layout; boards are flat slabs with no frame, legs or LED/material read.
critique: The graphic design is a strength. Fictional brands (Halcyon, Tidewater, Kestrel Bank, Lumen Sport, Volta, Meridian Tyres) have plausible logotypes and taglines, and the corner screen has team names, score and clock with legible typography on a lattice support. Shortfalls: (1) The perimeter boards are thin rectangular slabs, apparently sitting directly on the grass. The foreground 'Halcyon' board has no visible support legs, frame, rear prop or padding. Real perimeter boards are either 0.9 m padded A-frame boards or LED boards on a steel chassis, with a visible frame edge, rear legs and cable runs. (2) The boards are a single matte print with no LED pixel structure, no vinyl sheen, no wrinkles and no mud splash at the base. (3) The scoreboard housing is a plain black box. It needs a bezel, rear cabinet depth with vents, and a service walkway. Its screen is a perfectly clean flat image with no pixel pitch, glare or moiré. (4) Board heights and spacing are slightly inconsistent, and they all butt together with no gaps or joins.
suggestions: Board mesh: a 0.9 m high face with a 40 mm frame edge, angled rear A-frame legs or a box chassis, and a 50 mm foam top pad. Around 60-100 tris per 6 m board, instanced, with the graphic in an atlas.

For LED boards, add a subtle pixel-grid normal and a sub-pixel RGB texture visible only within ~10 m (use a mip bias), and an emissive at 1.5-2x. For printed boards, give the vinyl roughness 0.4 with a slight wrinkle normal.
Add a 100-150 mm mud splash and grass stain gradient at the base of the boards, plus 20-40 mm gaps and clamp brackets between boards.
Scoreboard: add a 150 mm bezel, a 0.6-0.8 m deep rear cabinet with louvres, a catwalk and handrail along the bottom, and a pixel-grid or glare treatment on the screen.
